LESSON 4 OF 4·Protect identity & access

Access Control & Authorization

Learn how web applications decide which users can access which data and perform which actions, including horizontal and vertical privilege boundaries.

Beginner24 min
Why this matters

Access control is the server-side decision about whether an already-identified user is allowed to access a resource or perform an action. A strong authorization model considers identity, role, resource, action, and context. Common failures include horizontal access-control problems where one user can access another user's data, and vertical privilege escalation where a lower-privileged user reaches administrative functionality.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Authentication establishes the identity associated with a request.
  • The application determines the requested resource and action.
  • The server evaluates policy using trusted identity and authorization data.
  • The server allows or denies the operation. The decision must happen at the protected resource or action, not only in the UI.
  • For object-level access, the authorization check must bind the requested object to the caller's actual permissions or ownership.

The background

As web applications moved from simple pages to multi-user systems and APIs, authorization became a major security boundary. OWASP Top 10:2025 lists Broken Access Control as A01. Modern ASVS 5.0 includes dedicated authorization requirements covering general authorization design, operation-level authorization, and other authorization considerations.

Real-world examples

  • PortSwigger's access-control material covers vertical and horizontal privilege escalation, IDOR, multi-step processes, URL and method-based controls, and prevention.
  • OWASP guidance emphasizes explicit authorization checks for each protected resource or action rather than relying on obscurity, client-side controls, or assumptions about how users navigate the application.

What to look for

  • Create a matrix of roles, users, resources, and sensitive actions.
  • Compare the same request using two authorized test accounts with different ownership or privilege levels.
  • Check direct object references such as user IDs, document IDs, order IDs, filenames, and account identifiers.
  • Test protected functions through their underlying HTTP requests rather than relying on whether a button is visible.
  • Review multi-step workflows and alternate HTTP methods for inconsistent authorization enforcement.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Access Control Labs

Choose an Apprentice-level access-control lab and compare requests made by users with different privileges or ownership.

Open PortSwigger resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Deny access by default to protected resources.
  • Enforce authorization server-side at the point where the resource or action is accessed.
  • Centralize authorization policy where practical so endpoints do not implement contradictory rules.
  • Bind object access to the authenticated principal and explicit permissions; never trust a client-supplied role or ownership field.
  • Test horizontal, vertical, and context-dependent authorization paths with negative cases.
  • Log important authorization failures and review them for abuse patterns.
